question: A customer bucket grows to hundreds of millions of blobs. What breaks first in GC and listing, and how would you fix it?
answer_hinglish:
Sabse pehle GC ka orphan scan tootega, listing nahi. `run_gc` do kaam karta hai: queued deletions (yeh scale karta hai, kyunki `blob_deletions` sirf delete hone wale keys rakhta hai, LIMIT 10000 per run) aur orphan scan. Orphan scan `storage.list_older_than(grace)` se POORE blob store ki listing leta hai, aur phir `SELECT blob_key FROM objects ... UNION SELECT blob_key FROM multipart_parts` se har referenced key ek Python set mein load karta hai. Observation (O6): yeh O(total blobs) per run hai -- 100 million keys ka set memory mein, aur S3 pe 1000-1000 karke list karna ghanton lagega. Worker har 300 second chalta hai, toh run khatam hi nahi hoga.

Listing ka path theek hai: `list_objects` `ix_objects_list (bucket, key text_pattern_ops)` partial index pe range scan karta hai aur `LIMIT max_keys + 1` leta hai, toh ek page ka cost bucket size se independent hai (assuming planner index use kare -- observation O8, EXPLAIN se check karna chahiye collation ki wajah se).

Fix: orphan scan ko incremental banao. Blob keys random hex hain, toh keyspace ko prefix shards (00..ff) mein baanto, har run ek shard scan kare. Har shard ke liye referenced set DB se usi prefix ke saath nikalo (`blob_key LIKE 'ab%'`, `ix_objects_blob` index use hoga). Ya better: orphan detection ko "intent log" se replace karo -- upload start pe `pending_blobs` row likho, commit pe hata do; GC sirf purane pending rows dekhe. Tab full scan ki zaroorat hi nahi.
why_needed: Orphan scan correctness ke liye zaroori hai (crash ke baad garbage), lekin uska cost bucket size ke saath linearly badhta hai -- production mein yahi pehla wall hai.
real_world_analogy: Godown ka stock-check: har mahine poora godown gin-na (full scan) chhote godown mein chalta hai; bade godown mein aisle-by-aisle rotation ya entry register (intent log) chahiye.
how_it_works: `list_older_than` local adapter pe `root.glob('*/*/*')` aur S3 pe paginated `list_objects_v2` karta hai. Phir har candidate ko `referenced` set ke against check karke `delete_any` hota hai. Queued path alag hai: `blob_deletions` se 10000 keys, har ek ke liye reference re-check, phir delete.
in_this_project: `objstore/services/maintenance.py::run_gc` mein `candidates = await storage.list_older_than(orphan_grace_seconds)` aur `referenced = set(...)` -- dono full-size hain. `storage/s3.py::list_older_than` `MaxKeys: 1000` ke saath ContinuationToken loop chalata hai. Listing `services/objects.py::list_objects` page-bounded hai. `DEPLOYMENT.md` bhi kehta hai ki `blob_deletions` growth aur GC failure pe alert lagao.
code_example:
# real, trimmed: objstore/services/maintenance.py (run_gc, orphan part)
candidates = await storage.list_older_than(orphan_grace_seconds)
async with sm() as s:
    referenced = set((await s.execute(text(
        "SELECT blob_key FROM objects WHERE blob_key IS NOT NULL UNION "
        "SELECT blob_key FROM multipart_parts"))).scalars().all())
for name in candidates:
    if name not in referenced:
        await storage.delete_any(name)
advantages: Current design simple aur correct hai chhote/medium scale pe
Listing page cost bucket size se independent
disadvantages: Orphan scan O(total blobs) time + memory
S3 listing bahut slow aur paid API calls
Ek run khatam hone se pehle agla schedule aa sakta hai
common_mistakes: Listing aur GC ko ek hi problem samajhna -- listing index-backed hai, GC nahi
Grace period hata ke scan fast karna -- in-flight uploads delete ho jayenge
Referenced set ko per-candidate query se replace karna bina index ke
follow_up_questions: How would an intent log (pending_blobs) replace the orphan scan?
How do AWS S3 Inventory reports help with this kind of reconciliation?
How would you shard the GC across several workers safely?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Full scan = simple aur self-healing (koi bhi garbage pakad leta hai); intent log = fast lekin ek extra write per upload aur extra table.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar GC run timeout ho ya OOM ho, worker `maintenance_failed` log karke sleep karega -- orphans kabhi saaf nahi honge aur storage cost chupke se badhegi.
advanced.alternatives: Prefix-sharded incremental scan; pending_blobs intent table; blob store inventory files (S3 Inventory) ko offline DB ke saath diff karna; blob store lifecycle tags.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 10x: prefix sharding kaafi hai. 100x: intent log + inventory-based weekly reconciliation, GC multiple workers mein shard by prefix with advisory locks.
advanced.production_improvements: GC metrics (scanned, orphans, duration) export karo, run time pe alert, orphan scan ko queued-deletion path se alag schedule karo.

question: Why does put_object wrap the metadata commit in `except BaseException` and delete the blob?
answer_hinglish:
Kyunki us point pe blob already storage mein likha ja chuka hai lekin abhi koi metadata use reference nahi karta. Agar digest check fail ho (BadDigest), quota exceed ho (QuotaExceeded), DB error aaye, ya client disconnect ho aur task cancel ho -- toh woh blob ek orphan ban jayega. Isliye `except BaseException:` mein `await storage.delete(blob_key)` aur phir `raise`. Exception swallow nahi hoti, sirf cleanup hota hai.

`Exception` ke bajaye `BaseException` kyun? asyncio mein request cancel hone pe `asyncio.CancelledError` aata hai, jo Python 3.8+ mein `BaseException` ka subclass hai, `Exception` ka nahi. Agar sirf `except Exception` likhte toh cancellation pe cleanup skip ho jata. KeyboardInterrupt bhi isi category mein hai.

Yeh "best effort" hai: agar delete khud fail ho jaye (S3 down), toh blob orphan reh jata hai -- lekin yahi toh GC ka orphan scan pakadta hai grace period ke baad. Toh do layers: fast path pe turant cleanup, aur safety net GC. Important baat: blob_key random aur naya hai, toh is blob ko delete karna kabhi kisi live object ko nahi chhoo sakta.
why_needed: Failed uploads ko storage leak nahi banna chahiye; turant cleanup storage cost bachata hai aur GC pe load kam karta hai.
real_world_analogy: Restaurant mein order cancel hua toh plate jo bana li thi turant hata do; agar bhool gaye toh raat ko safai wala (GC) utha lega.
how_it_works: Flow: `storage.put` (bytes) -> `_verify_digests` -> transaction (advisory lock, optional quota, `commit_version`). Inme se kahin bhi exception -> blob delete -> exception re-raise -> bpcommon error handler usko JSON error mein convert karta hai (400 BadDigest, 403 QuotaExceeded, 500 ...).
in_this_project: `objstore/services/objects.py::put_object` -- `try: _verify_digests(...); async with sm() as s, s.begin(): ...` aur `except BaseException: await storage.delete(blob_key); raise`. Test `test_integrity_checks_reject_corrupted_uploads` assert karta hai ki `list((tmp_path / "blobs").glob("*/*/*")) == []` -- yaani rejected blob disk pe nahi bacha. `upload_part` aur `complete_multipart` mein bhi same pattern hai.
code_example:
# real, trimmed: objstore/services/objects.py (put_object)
try:
    _verify_digests(info, content_md5, sha256_header, signed_sha256)
    async with sm() as s, s.begin():
        await s.execute(text(key_lock_sql()), {"b": bucket["name"], "k": key})
        ...
        vid = await commit_version(s, bucket, key, blob_key=blob_key, ...)
except BaseException:
    await storage.delete(blob_key)   # nothing references it; best effort (GC catches failures)
    raise
advantages: Exception type preserve hota hai (bare raise)
disadvantages: Cleanup khud fail ho sakta hai -- GC zaroori
Commit succeed hone ke baad ack lost ho toh bhi yeh path nahi chalta (correct hai)
common_mistakes: `except Exception` likhna aur CancelledError miss karna
Exception swallow karke 200 return karna
Commit ke BAAD wale error pe bhi blob delete kar dena (tab woh live hai)
follow_up_questions: Why is CancelledError a BaseException in modern Python?
What if the COMMIT succeeds but the connection drops before the client sees it?
Why does storage.put failure (TooLarge) take a different branch?

question: Why do object routes use `{key:path}` and what does `_check_key` enforce?
answer_hinglish:
Object key mein slash hota hai -- `2026/trip/beach.jpg` ek hi key hai. FastAPI ka normal `{key}` path parameter sirf ek segment match karta hai (slash pe ruk jata hai), toh `/buckets/photos/objects/2026/trip/beach.jpg` 404 deta. `{key:path}` Starlette ka path converter hai jo baaki poora path (slashes ke saath) ek string mein de deta hai. Isse flat namespace ka "folder" illusion bina kisi special handling ke chal jata hai.

`_check_key` do cheezein check karta hai: key empty na ho, aur UTF-8 encoded length 1024 bytes se zyada na ho (S3 ka bhi yahi limit hai). Bytes count karna zaroori hai, characters nahi -- emoji 4 bytes ka hota hai. Isse bahut lambi keys index aur URL limits ko nahi todti.

Note karo key ke content pe koi restriction nahi: `../../etc/passwd`, spaces, `%`, backslash -- sab valid data hai, kyunki key kabhi filesystem path nahi banti (blob key random hai). Path ke liye safety client side `quote_key` se aati hai jo dot segments ko `%2E` bana deta hai, warna HTTP client URL normalise kar deta.
why_needed: Keys mein slashes aur arbitrary bytes allowed hone chahiye, lekin size bounded rehna chahiye.
real_world_analogy: Library mein book ka poora catalogue number '2026/Fiction/A-12' ek hi label hai -- shelf ka naam nahi.
how_it_works: Starlette path converter regex `.*` use karta hai. Route `@router.put("/buckets/{bucket}/objects/{key:path}")` -> `key` mein decoded path. `_check_key` `len(key.encode()) > 1024` pe `Unprocessable` (422) raise karta hai. Multipart initiate route (`/uploads/{key:path}`) bhi `_check_key` call karta hai.
in_this_project: `objstore/api/routes.py::_check_key` aur `put_object` / `initiate` routes. Test `test_hostile_keys_never_touch_filesystem_paths` keys jaise `"emoji/\U0001F600.txt"`, `"spaces and %25 and ?q=1"`, `"../../etc/passwd"` round trip karta hai. GET/HEAD/DELETE `_check_key` call nahi karte -- woh bas lookup karte hain, invalid key ka row hoga hi nahi.
advantages: Slash wali keys naturally kaam karti hain
Byte-based limit Unicode ke saath sahi
disadvantages: Path converter trailing slash wali keys pe dhyan maangta hai
Validation sirf write routes pe hai
common_mistakes: `{key}` use karna aur slashes tod dena
len(key) characters mein count karna
Key ke content ko sanitize karna (`..` hata dena) -- yeh data badal deta hai
follow_up_questions: How does the client make sure `..` segments reach the server unchanged?
Should keys with control characters be rejected?
Why is 1024 bytes a sensible limit for an indexed text column?

question: How does ObjClient sign a request, and why does it send UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD for streamed bodies?
answer_hinglish:
`ObjClient` woh kaam karta hai jo boto3 S3 ke liye karta hai: request build karo, phir uske exact bytes ke upar signature lagao. `request()` pehle `httpx.build_request` se request banata hai, taaki URL wahi encoding le jo wire pe jayega. Phir `req.url.raw_path` se raw (percent-encoded) path nikalta hai -- server bhi `scope["raw_path"]` se hi verify karta hai, toh dono same string sign karte hain. Query `req.url.query` se, aur `sign_headers` `Authorization`, `x-obj-date`, `x-obj-content-sha256` headers set karta hai.

Body: agar content bytes hai toh `sha256(body)` sign hota hai -- server pe `signed_sha256` banta hai aur `_verify_digests` usko actual body se compare karta hai, toh beech mein body swap pakda jata hai. Lekin agar content async iterator (stream) hai, toh client ke paas poori body sign karne ke liye pehle se nahi hai -- use buffer ya do baar padhna padega. Isliye `body=None` -> `UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD`. Tab body integrity Content-MD5 / checksum header aur TLS pe depend karti hai.

`put()` default mein Content-MD5 bhi bhejta hai (`md5=True`), jo transit corruption pakadta hai. Benchmark `md5=False` use karta hai.
why_needed: Client aur server ko byte-for-byte same canonical string banana hai, warna 401; streams ke liye double hashing avoid karna hai.
real_world_analogy: Cheque pe amount aur payee dono likh ke sign karna (signed payload) vs blank amount wala signed cheque jahan amount alag se verify hota hai (unsigned payload).
how_it_works: `sign_headers(ak, sk, method, raw_path, query, body)` -> date = now, sha = sha256(body) ya UNSIGNED, sig = HMAC(secret, METHOD/RAW_PATH/CANONICAL_QUERY/DATE/SHA). Server `authenticate` same string recompute karke `hmac.compare_digest` karta hai.
in_this_project: `objstore/client.py::ObjClient.request` -- `body = req.content if (sign_body and not hasattr(content, "__aiter__")) else None` aur `raw_path = req.url.raw_path.decode().split("?")[0]`. `put()` keys ko `quote_key` se encode karta hai. `test_signed_body_cannot_be_swapped` signed sha256 ke saath tampered body bhejta hai -> 400 BadDigest.
code_example:
# real, trimmed: objstore/client.py
async def request(self, method, path, *, params=None, content=None, json=None, headers=None, sign_body=True):
    req = self.http.build_request(method, path, params=params, content=content, json=json, headers=headers)
    body = req.content if (sign_body and not hasattr(content, "__aiter__")) else None
    raw_path = req.url.raw_path.decode().split("?")[0]
    req.headers.update(sign_headers(self.ak, self.sk, method, raw_path, req.url.query.decode(), body))
    return await self.http.send(req)
advantages: Signs exactly what goes on the wire
disadvantages: UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD pe proxy body swap signature se nahi pakdega
Client clock skew 15 min se zyada ho toh 401
common_mistakes: Decoded path sign karna jabki server raw path verify karta hai
Query ko sort kiye bina sign karna
Body sign karne ke liye 5GB file memory mein padh lena
follow_up_questions: How does AWS solve streaming with signed payloads (chunked signing)?
Why does the client need quote_key for dot segments?
What would break if the client used local time that is 20 minutes off?

question: How is user metadata (`x-obj-meta-*`) stored and returned?
answer_hinglish:
Client koi bhi custom header `x-obj-meta-<name>: <value>` PUT ke saath bhej sakta hai -- jaise `x-obj-meta-camera: x100`. Server prefix hata ke `{"camera": "x100"}` dict banata hai aur `objects.user_metadata` jsonb column mein store karta hai. GET/HEAD pe `_object_headers` us dict ko wapas `x-obj-meta-camera` headers mein badal deta hai. S3 mein bhi exactly yahi pattern hai (`x-amz-meta-*`).

Important: metadata version ke saath immutable hai. Metadata badalna hai toh naya PUT (naya version) karna padta hai -- in-place update nahi. Multipart mein metadata initiate ke time pe `multipart_uploads.user_metadata` mein save hota hai aur complete ke time version pe copy hota hai.

Dhyan dene wali baat: HTTP header names case-insensitive hain, toh keys lowercase mein aati hain (Starlette headers lowercase deta hai). Aur headers ka total size proxies pe limited hota hai (typically 8KB jaise ballpark), toh metadata chhota rakhna chahiye -- bade data ke liye object hi use karo.
why_needed: Objects ke saath app-specific info (camera, uploader, original filename) bina alag database ke rakhni hoti hai.
real_world_analogy: Parcel pe chipka sticker: andar ka saamaan (bytes) nahi badalta, sticker pe extra info likhi hoti hai.
how_it_works: PUT: `_meta_headers(request)` -> dict -> `put_object(metadata=...)` -> `commit_version` -> `CAST(:md AS jsonb)`. GET: `head_object` row -> `_object_headers(row)` -> `for k, v in row["user_metadata"].items(): h[f"x-obj-meta-{k}"] = v`.
in_this_project: `objstore/api/routes.py::_meta_headers` aur `_object_headers`; column `user_metadata jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'` in `migrations/versions/0001_initial.py`. Test `test_put_get_roundtrip_metadata_and_etag` `meta={"camera": "x100"}` bhejta hai aur `g.headers["x-obj-meta-camera"] == "x100"` assert karta hai.
disadvantages: Header size limits
Metadata pe query/search ka index nahi
Non-ASCII values headers mein tricky
common_mistakes: Metadata ko case-sensitive maan lena
Badi JSON metadata headers mein bhejna
Metadata update ke liye in-place UPDATE ki ummeed karna

What is the difference between user metadata and system metadata like Content-Type?

question: Why does canonical_query sort and percent-encode query parameters before signing?
answer_hinglish:
Signature tabhi verify ho sakta hai jab client aur server bilkul same string ka HMAC nikalein. Query string ke saath problem yeh hai ki same meaning ki kai representations hain: `a=1&b=2` aur `b=2&a=1` same hain; `%2F` aur `/`, ya space ka `+` vs `%20` -- different bytes, same meaning. Agar raw query sign karte, toh koi proxy ya HTTP library order ya encoding badal de toh signature fail.

`canonical_query` ek canonical form banata hai: `parse_qsl(..., keep_blank_values=True)` se decode, `sorted()` se key/value order fix, phir `quote(k, safe='-_.~')` se ek fixed encoding (RFC 3986 unreserved characters chhod ke sab encode). Dono side yahi function call karti hain, toh representation ka farak mit jata hai.

`exclude` parameter presigned URLs ke liye hai: `X-Obj-Signature` khud signature ka hissa nahi ho sakta (chicken-and-egg), isliye canonical query se bahar. Lekin `X-Obj-Credential` aur `X-Obj-Expires` andar hain -- toh expiry badal ke URL lamba nahi kar sakte. `keep_blank_values` zaroori hai warna `?versions=` jaisa param chupke se drop ho jata.
why_needed: Canonicalisation ke bina harmless re-encoding se valid requests reject hongi, ya worse, do alag requests same signature share karengi.
real_world_analogy: Do log ek shopping list compare kar rahe hain -- pehle dono alphabetically sort karo, tab line-by-line match karo.
how_it_works:
`string_to_sign = METHOD 
 RAW_PATH 
 canonical_query(query) 
 DATE 
 SHA`. Presign: `canonical_query(q, {"X-Obj-Signature"})` + `"PRESIGNED"` + expires. Server `presigned_string` same exclude ke saath recompute karta hai.
in_this_project: `objstore/services/signing.py::canonical_query`, `string_to_sign`, `presign`, `presigned_string`. `test_presigned_urls` key badalne pe 401 assert karta hai; `test_auth_failures` different path pe replay 401.
disadvantages: Path canonicalised nahi -- raw path exactly match hona chahiye
Duplicate keys sort ho jate hain lekin semantics app pe depend
common_mistakes: Signature param ko hi sign karne ki koshish
keep_blank_values bhool jana
Client aur server mein alag quote safe sets
follow_up_questions: Why is the path signed raw instead of canonicalised?
How does AWS SigV4 canonicalise headers as well?

question: In upload_part, why is a re-uploaded part handled with ON CONFLICT upsert, and why is the old part's blob queued instead of deleted?
answer_hinglish:
Multipart ka main promise hai "failed part ko dobara bhejo". Client same `part_number` ke saath retry karega -- kabhi isliye ki pehla attempt fail hua, kabhi isliye ki pehla succeed hua tha par response kho gaya. Dono case mein server ko last upload ko winner banana hai. `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (upload_id, part_number) DO UPDATE SET size, etag, blob_key, uploaded_at = now()` ek atomic upsert hai: koi "pehle check karo, phir insert ya update" race nahi.

Purana blob turant delete kyun nahi? Kyunki delete transaction ke andar storage call hoti -- agar transaction baad mein rollback ho jaye toh row purane blob ko point karegi jo delete ho chuka hai (dangling metadata). Isliye project ka rule: metadata transaction ke andar sirf `_queue_blob_deletion(s, old)` -- yeh bhi same transaction ka hissa hai, rollback hua toh queue entry bhi gayi. Commit hua toh GC baad mein `blob_deletions` se uthayega, aur delete se pehle re-check karega ki koi `objects` ya `multipart_parts` row ab bhi use reference toh nahi karta.

Review fix (O2): pehle yahan `_check_quota` bucket `FOR UPDATE` lock ke bina chalta tha, toh concurrent part uploads quota se aage nikal sakte the. Ab quota'd bucket pe part upload bhi `SELECT 1 FROM buckets WHERE name = :b FOR UPDATE` leta hai, `put_object` jaisa (`test_multipart_parts_respect_quota_and_completion_check_is_real`).
why_needed: Retries idempotent-ish aur crash-safe hone chahiye, aur storage deletion kabhi metadata se aage nahi jana chahiye.
real_world_analogy: Exam mein answer sheet ka page dobara likha -- naya page staple karo, purana page 'shred' tray mein daalo; shredder baad mein confirm karke shred karega.
how_it_works: upload_part: upload exist check -> naya random blob stream -> Content-MD5 verify -> txn: upload re-check, quota check, old blob_key select, upsert, old blob queue -> commit. Fail pe naya blob delete.
in_this_project: `objstore/services/objects.py::upload_part` -- `old = SELECT blob_key FROM multipart_parts WHERE upload_id = :u AND part_number = :n`, phir upsert, phir `_queue_blob_deletion(s, old)`. Primary key `(upload_id, part_number)` migration mein hai. Test `test_multipart_upload` part 2 ko `b"b" * 10` se re-upload karta hai aur final content mein naya part aata hai.
code_example:
# real, trimmed: objstore/services/objects.py (upload_part)
old = (await s.execute(text("SELECT blob_key FROM multipart_parts WHERE upload_id = :u AND part_number = :n"),
                       {"u": upload_id, "n": part_number})).scalar()
await s.execute(text(
    "INSERT INTO multipart_parts (upload_id, part_number, size, etag, blob_key) VALUES (:u, :n, :sz, :e, :bk) "
    "ON CONFLICT (upload_id, part_number) DO UPDATE SET size = EXCLUDED.size, etag = EXCLUDED.etag, "
    "blob_key = EXCLUDED.blob_key, uploaded_at = now()"), {...})
await _queue_blob_deletion(s, old)
disadvantages: Two concurrent uploads of the same part: last commit wins, dusre ka blob queue hota hai (fine, but wasted I/O)
Quota'd buckets pe parts bhi bucket lock pe serialize (review fix ka cost)
common_mistakes: Transaction ke andar storage.delete call karna
Old blob_key ko upsert ke BAAD select karna (tab naya mil jayega)
Retry ko naye part_number ke saath bhejna
follow_up_questions: Is the SELECT-then-upsert racy between two concurrent retries of the same part?
How would you fix the quota race in upload_part?
Why does GC re-check references before deleting a queued blob?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Queue-based deletion ek extra table aur GC dependency laata hai, lekin metadata/data ordering kabhi nahi tootta.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Do concurrent same-part retries: dono `old` = pehla blob padh sakte hain; ek ka naya blob overwritten ho jata hai aur kabhi queue nahi hota -> orphan, jo orphan scan grace ke baad hatata hai.
advanced.alternatives: Part row pe `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` ya part-level advisory lock; ya `RETURNING` ke saath old value capture karne ke liye CTE.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Hazaron parallel parts pe quota sum query (sum over all objects + parts) har part pe mehngi -- counters table chahiye.
advanced.production_improvements: Bucket lock (done, O2) ki jagah scale pe usage counter row; `old` capture ko CTE se atomic banao; per-part metrics.

question: If you replaced the S3 backend with your own blob layer, how would you add durability through replication or erasure coding?
answer_hinglish:
Seedha jawab: is project mein yeh implement nahi hai -- durability S3-compatible backend (SeaweedFS / MinIO / AWS) ko delegate ki gayi hai, README ki known limitations mein likha hai "no replication/erasure coding". Production mein apna blob layer banana ho toh aise karte:

Replication (simple): har blob ko 3 storage nodes pe likho, alag failure domains (rack/AZ) mein. Write tab successful jab write quorum (jaise 2 of 3) ack kare; read kisi bhi healthy replica se, checksum verify karke. Cost: 3x storage.

Erasure coding (efficient): blob ko k data chunks mein todo aur m parity chunks banao (Reed-Solomon), jaise 8+4. Koi bhi 8 chunks se poora blob reconstruct ho jata hai, toh 4 nodes tak loss bardasht; storage overhead sirf 1.5x. Cost: CPU encode/decode, aur chhoti files pe bahut chunks -- isliye chhote objects ko pack karke bade "volumes" mein rakhte hain (Haystack / SeaweedFS ka idea).

Background repair: scrubber har chunk ka checksum periodically verify kare, aur missing chunks rebuild kare. Hamara SHA-256 per object already end-to-end check deta hai.

Achhi baat: hamare design mein `StorageAdapter` protocol hai -- metadata ko pata hi nahi bytes kaise store hain, toh naya adapter plug ho sakta hai bina API badle.
why_needed: Disks aur nodes fail hote hain; ek copy wala blob store data loss guarantee karta hai.
real_world_analogy: Important document ki 3 photocopies teen alag shehron mein (replication) vs ek puzzle ke tukde jisme koi bhi 8 of 12 tukde poori picture bana dein (erasure coding).
how_it_works: Write path: chunking -> encode -> parallel writes to k+m nodes -> placement map (blob_key -> nodes) metadata mein -> ack. Read path: k chunks fetch (parallel, fastest first), decode, verify checksum. Repair: scrub, detect, rebuild on a new node, update placement.
in_this_project: `objstore/storage/base.py::StorageAdapter` (put/get/delete/exists/list_older_than) wahi seam hai jahan naya `ReplicatedAdapter` ya `ErasureCodedAdapter` aata. `storage/s3.py::S3Adapter` aaj durability backend ko deta hai; `SYSTEM_DESIGN.md` "erasure coding in the blob layer" ko huge-object scaling step ke roop mein list karta hai. `objects.sha256` integrity scrub ke liye reuse ho sakta hai.
disadvantages: Apna blob layer banana bahut bada operational kaam
EC chhote objects pe inefficient

question: Design server-side multipart composition so completion does not re-stream all the bytes.
answer_hinglish:
Aaj `complete_multipart` saare parts ko `storage.get` se padh ke ek naye blob mein `storage.put` karta hai -- yaani 5GB object ke liye completion pe 5GB read + 5GB write, aur client ka complete request tab tak latka rehta hai. TRADEOFFS.md is cheez ko "doubles I/O at completion" bolta hai. Server-side composition is project mein implement nahi hai; production mein aise karte:

Option 1 -- manifest object: final object ka metadata ek list of (part blob_key, size) ban jaye. Completion sirf ek DB transaction hai: parts ko "owned by version X" mark karo, ETag compute karo (already md5-of-md5s hai), done -- O(1) data movement. GET pe ek concatenating reader parts ko sequence mein stream karta hai; Range request ke liye cumulative offsets se sahi part aur offset dhundho. Iske liye `objects` table mein `blob_key` ki jagah `object_parts (object_id, seq, blob_key, offset, size)` chahiye, aur GC reference check us table ko bhi dekhe.

Option 2 -- backend native: S3 backend pe khud S3 multipart use karo (`create_multipart_upload`, `upload_part`, `complete_multipart_upload`) -- backend compose karta hai. Lekin local adapter mein yeh nahi hai, toh adapter protocol mein optional `compose()` capability chahiye.

SHA-256 ka issue: full-object SHA-256 bina bytes padhe nahi milta -- ya toh per-part checksums store karo (S3 bhi "checksum of checksums" deta hai), ya background job baad mein compute kare.
why_needed: Bade objects pe completion latency aur double I/O bekaar cost hai; real S3 completion fast hota hai.
real_world_analogy: Kitaab ke chapters alag-alag file mein -- nayi copy chhapne ke bajaye ek table of contents (manifest) bana do jo chapters ko order mein point kare.
how_it_works: Manifest approach: complete txn -> lock key -> delete upload row -> insert object row with manifest -> unused parts queue for deletion. GET -> manifest -> ordered part streams. Delete -> sab part blobs queue.
in_this_project: Aaj ka code: `objstore/services/objects.py::complete_multipart` mein `async def concatenated(): for p in chosen: async for chunk in storage.get(p.blob_key): yield chunk` aur `storage.put(final_blob, HashingStream(concatenated(), ...))`. `README.md` known limitation: "Multipart completion re-streams the parts into a new blob (real S3 composes server-side)". ETag line `hashlib.md5(b"".join(bytes.fromhex(p.etag) for p in chosen)).hexdigest() + f"-{len(chosen)}"` bytes nahi padhti, toh manifest design mein as-is chalegi.

# real, trimmed: objstore/services/objects.py (today: re-streaming)
async def concatenated():
    for p in chosen:
        async for chunk in storage.get(p.blob_key):
            yield chunk

final_blob = new_blob_key()
info = await storage.put(final_blob, HashingStream(concatenated(), sum(p.size for p in chosen)))

question: How would you add object lock / WORM retention to this system?
answer_hinglish:
Is project mein object lock implement nahi hai -- SECURITY.md gaps mein "no object lock / WORM" likha hai. Abhi bucket owner (ya admin) `DELETE ?versionId=` se koi bhi version permanently mita sakta hai, aur lifecycle bhi. Ransomware ya compromised key ke case mein backups bhi gayab ho sakte hain.

Production mein aise karte: versioning mandatory karo (lock sirf versioned bucket pe, S3 ki tarah). `objects` mein do columns: `retain_until timestamptz` aur `legal_hold boolean`. Bucket pe default retention rule (jaise 30 days, mode governance/compliance).

Enforcement points -- yahi important hai:
1. `delete_object` with versionId: agar `retain_until > now()` ya legal_hold -> 403 (compliance mode mein admin bhi nahi; governance mein special permission se bypass).
2. `commit_version` disabled/suspended path jo 'null' version ko DELETE karta hai -- locked null version ko overwrite nahi hone dena.
3. Lifecycle noncurrent expiration aur lone-marker cleanup ki bulk SQL mein `AND (retain_until IS NULL OR retain_until < now()) AND NOT legal_hold`.
4. GC: blob_deletions mein locked blob kabhi aana hi nahi chahiye -- defence in depth ke liye GC bhi check kare.
Delete marker lagana allowed rehta hai (data recoverable rehta hai), sirf permanent delete block hota hai.

Retention badhana allowed, ghatana sirf governance mode mein. Clock: DB ka `now()` use karo, client ka nahi.
why_needed: Compliance (SEC 17a-4 jaise rules) aur ransomware protection ke liye kuch data ko fixed time tak undeletable rakhna padta hai.
real_world_analogy: Bank locker jiska time-lock hai -- chabi hone ke bawajood 30 din se pehle nahi khulega.
how_it_works: Har destructive path (version delete, null overwrite, lifecycle, GC) ek common predicate se guard hota hai `is_locked(row, now)`. Settings change (retention shorten) bhi audit log ke saath.
in_this_project: Aaj ke destructive paths: `objstore/services/objects.py::delete_object` (`DELETE FROM objects ... AND version_id = :v`), `commit_version` (null row DELETE), `objstore/services/maintenance.py::run_lifecycle` (bulk DELETE with `lag()`), aur `run_gc`. Bucket config routes (`set_versioning`, `set_lifecycle`) `objstore/api/routes.py` mein -- wahi naya `PUT /buckets/{b}/object-lock` jata.
code_example:
# illustrative (NOT in repo): guard inside delete_object before the permanent DELETE
row = (await s.execute(text(
    "SELECT retain_until, legal_hold FROM objects WHERE bucket = :b AND key = :k AND version_id = :v"),
    {"b": bucket["name"], "k": key, "v": version_id})).first()
if row and (row.legal_hold or (row.retain_until and row.retain_until > now_db)):
    raise Forbidden("object version is locked", details={"code": "AccessDenied", "retain_until": str(row.retain_until)})

disadvantages: Storage cost: locked data quota/billing mein rehta hai
Galat retention set hua toh compliance mode mein undo nahi
Har destructive path pe check -- ek bhi miss = bypass
common_mistakes: Sirf API delete pe check lagana, lifecycle/GC bhool jana
Client clock se retention compare karna
Unversioned bucket pe lock allow karna (overwrite = data loss)

advanced.failure_scenarios: Ek missed path (jaise null-version overwrite) lock bypass kar deta hai; DB admin direct SQL se bhi mita sakta hai -- isliye true WORM ke liye blob layer (S3 Object Lock) pe bhi lock chahiye.

question: How would you add server-side encryption, and how would envelope encryption with a KMS fit this design?
answer_hinglish:
Is project mein server-side encryption (SSE) implement nahi hai -- SECURITY.md gaps mein "no server-side encryption of blobs" aur "access key secrets stored in plaintext" dono hain; DEPLOYMENT.md checklist bolta hai "Encrypt access key secrets and, if required, blobs at rest (SSE)". Production mein aise karte:

Envelope encryption: har object (ya version) ke liye ek random data key (DEK, AES-256) banao. Bytes ko DEK se encrypt karo -- streaming ke liye AES-GCM per chunk (jaise 64KB chunks, har chunk ka apna nonce aur tag) taaki Range GET bhi kaam kare aur poora object memory mein na aaye. DEK ko KMS ki master key (KEK) se encrypt (wrap) karo aur wrapped DEK `objects` row mein store karo. Master key kabhi KMS se bahar nahi aati.

Kyun envelope? 5GB data KMS ko bhejna impossible; sirf 32-byte DEK wrap/unwrap hota hai. Key rotation sasti: KEK rotate karo toh sirf wrapped DEKs re-wrap, data re-encrypt nahi.

Is codebase mein fit: `HashingStream` ki tarah ek `EncryptingStream` jo `storage.put` se pehle wrap kare, aur `storage.get` ke baad decrypting generator. Important: MD5/SHA-256 plaintext pe compute ho (client ETag compare karta hai), toh hashing encryption se pehle. Range: requested plaintext range ko chunk boundaries pe align karke ciphertext range fetch karo.

Access key secrets ke liye bhi same: secret ko KMS se encrypt karke store, aur `_secret` cache mein decrypted rakho.
why_needed: Disk/backup chori ya blob store compromise pe data readable nahi hona chahiye; compliance (PCI, HIPAA) maangta hai.
real_world_analogy: Har locker ki apni chabi (DEK), aur saari chabiyan ek master safe (KMS) mein band -- safe ki master chabi kabhi bahar nahi aati.
how_it_works: PUT: plaintext -> HashingStream (md5/sha) -> EncryptingStream(DEK) -> adapter. Metadata: wrapped_dek, key_id, chunk_size. GET: unwrap DEK (KMS call, cacheable) -> ciphertext range -> decrypt chunks -> trim to requested plaintext range.
in_this_project: Seams: `objstore/storage/base.py::HashingStream` (wrapping stream pattern), `objstore/services/objects.py::put_object` (jahan stream banta hai), `objstore/api/routes.py::get_object` (`storage.get(row["blob_key"], start, end)`), aur `objstore/services/auth.py::_secret` (plaintext `secret` column). Migration comment: `secret text NOT NULL -- needed to verify HMACs (like AWS); encrypt at rest in production`.
advantages: Blob store compromise pe data safe
disadvantages: CPU cost har byte pe
Range GET complex (chunk alignment)
KMS availability critical dependency
common_mistakes: Poore object ka ek GCM tag -- Range aur streaming toot jata hai
Hash ciphertext pe compute karna (ETag mismatch)
Nonce reuse same DEK ke saath
follow_up_questions: Why is envelope encryption preferred over encrypting everything directly with KMS?
How does key rotation work without re-encrypting data?
What is SSE-C and why would a customer want it?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: SSE-S3 style (hum keys manage karein) vs SSE-KMS (customer audit/control) vs SSE-C (customer key, hum store nahi karte). Zyada control = zyada operational complexity.
advanced.failure_scenarios: KMS down -> koi encrypted object read nahi hoga; wrapped DEK kho gaya -> data permanently lost. DEK cache leak = us object ka data exposed.
advanced.alternatives: Backend ka native SSE (S3/MinIO) on karna -- simplest, lekin blob store admin ke against protection nahi; client-side encryption.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 100x pe KMS call rate limit -- DEK unwrap results cache karo (short TTL), ya per-bucket data keys.
advanced.production_improvements: Pehle secrets ko KMS se encrypt karo (sabse bada gap), phir backend SSE on, phir agar zaroorat ho toh app-level envelope encryption.

question: Write a test proving that after a DELETE in a versioned bucket, GET and HEAD return 404 with the delete-marker header, but GET with the old versionId still returns the data.
answer_hinglish:
Test ka goal hai delete marker semantics pin karna: versioned bucket mein DELETE data nahi mitata, sirf ek naya "latest" version (marker) banata hai. Toh teen cheezein assert karni hain: (1) plain GET 404 aur `x-obj-delete-marker: true` header, (2) HEAD bhi 404 deta hai (body nahi hoti lekin status aur headers same logic `head_object` se aate hain), (3) `versionId=<v1>` ke saath GET purana data deta hai -- proof ki bytes abhi bhi stored hain.

Ek extra check jo achha signal deta hai: stats mein `delete_markers == 1` aur `all_versions == 1`, aur `stored_bytes` original size ke barabar -- yaani delete ne storage free nahi kiya (yahi quota mein surprise hota hai).

Repo ke existing helpers use karo: `server(tmp_path)` context manager jo app + signed clients deta hai, aur `bucket(c)` helper jo `photos` bucket banata hai. HEAD ke liye `a.request("HEAD", ...)` aur path `quote_key` se. Response header `x-obj-version-id` mein marker ka version id aata hai -- woh delete response JSON ke `version_id` se match hona chahiye.
why_needed: Versioning ke edge cases (marker, HEAD, versionId) regressions ke liye sabse fragile hote hain; test unhe lock karta hai.
real_world_analogy: Recycle bin check: file desktop se gayab dikhni chahiye, lekin recycle bin (version history) mein se khul sakti hai.
how_it_works: `delete_object` versioned bucket pe `commit_version(..., delete_marker=True)` call karta hai. `head_object` latest row dekhta hai; `is_delete_marker` pe `NotFound` with headers `x-obj-delete-marker`/`x-obj-version-id`. bpcommon error handler `exc.headers` response pe lagata hai.
in_this_project: Test `tests/test_objects.py` style mein likha jayega, `from .conftest import server` aur `bucket` helper ke saath. Existing `test_versioning_and_delete_markers` GET 404 check karta hai lekin HEAD aur stats nahi -- yeh test woh gap cover karta hai.

# solution: tests/test_objects.py (new test)
async def test_delete_marker_hides_object_but_versions_survive(db, tmp_path):
    async with server(tmp_path) as (app, cl, anon):
        a = cl["alice"]
        await bucket(a)
        await a.request("PUT", "/buckets/photos/versioning", json={"status": "enabled"})
        v1 = (await a.put("photos", "r.txt", b"report")).headers["x-obj-version-id"]
        d = (await a.delete("photos", "r.txt")).json()
        assert d["delete_marker"] is True

        g = await a.get("photos", "r.txt")
        assert g.status_code == 404 and g.headers["x-obj-delete-marker"] == "true"
        assert g.headers["x-obj-version-id"] == d["version_id"]

        h = await a.request("HEAD", f"/buckets/photos/objects/{quote_key('r.txt')}")
        assert h.status_code == 404 and h.headers["x-obj-delete-marker"] == "true"

        old = await a.get("photos", "r.txt", params={"versionId": v1})
        assert old.status_code == 200 and old.content == b"report"

        st = (await a.request("GET", "/buckets/photos/stats")).json()
        assert st["delete_markers"] == 1 and st["all_versions"] == 1 and st["stored_bytes"] == 6

question: Add `If-Match` support to PUT so a client can overwrite an object only if its current ETag matches (optimistic concurrency).
answer_hinglish:
Use case: do clients ek JSON config object edit kar rahe hain. Bina condition ke last writer wins aur ek ka change chupchap kho jata hai (lost update). `If-Match: "<etag>"` ke saath client kehta hai "overwrite tabhi karo jab current version wahi hai jo maine padha tha", warna 412 Precondition Failed. Observation (O9): aaj sirf GET pe single-ETag If-None-Match hai, If-Match nahi.

Sahi jagah check ki: transaction ke andar, per-key advisory lock lene ke BAAD. Agar lock se pehle check karte toh check aur commit ke beech doosra writer aa sakta tha (TOCTOU). Lock ke baad latest row stable hai, kyunki same key ke saare writers isi lock pe serialize hote hain.

Order bhi same rehta hai: bytes pehle stream ho chuke hain. Precondition fail hone pe exception `except BaseException` branch mein jati hai jo naya blob delete kar deti hai -- toh koi orphan nahi. Downside: client ne poora body upload kar diya aur phir 412 mila -- bade objects ke liye client pehle HEAD karke check kar sakta hai, lekin authoritative check commit ke time hi hai.

`If-Match: *` = "object exist karna chahiye"; latest delete marker hai toh woh "not exist" maana jayega.
why_needed: Read-modify-write workflows mein lost updates rokne ke liye; S3 ne bhi 2024 mein conditional writes add kiye.
real_world_analogy: Google Doc ka 'someone else edited this, reload first' warning -- aapka save tabhi jayega jab aapne latest version dekha ho.
how_it_works: Route header `if_match` padhta hai -> `put_object(if_match=...)` -> txn: key lock -> `SELECT etag, is_delete_marker FROM objects WHERE bucket AND key AND is_latest` -> compare -> mismatch pe `PreconditionFailed` (412) -> blob cleanup via existing except branch.
in_this_project: Changes: `objstore/services/objects.py` mein naya `PreconditionFailed(AppError)` (status 412), `put_object` mein `if_match` param aur lock ke baad check; `objstore/api/routes.py::put_object` mein `if_match: str | None = Header(default=None)` pass karna. Existing helper `key_lock_sql()` reuse.

    status_code, code = 412, "PreconditionFailed"

# inside put_object(..., if_match: str | None = None), in the transaction AFTER the key lock:
        async with sm() as s, s.begin():
            await s.execute(text(key_lock_sql()), {"b": bucket["name"], "k": key})
            if if_match is not None:
                cur = (await s.execute(text("SELECT etag, is_delete_marker FROM objects "
                                            "WHERE bucket = :b AND key = :k AND is_latest"),
                                       {"b": bucket["name"], "k": key})).first()
                exists = cur is not None and not cur.is_delete_marker
                ok = exists if if_match.strip() == "*" else (exists and cur.etag == if_match.strip().strip('"'))
                if not ok:
                    raise PreconditionFailed("If-Match does not match the current ETag")
            ...  # quota + commit_version unchanged

        h = {"if-match": e1}
        r1 = await a.request("PUT", "/buckets/photos/objects/cfg.json", content=b'{"a":1}', headers=h)
        r2 = await a.request("PUT", "/buckets/photos/objects/cfg.json", content=b'{"b":2}', headers=h)

question: Write a test that pages through a delimiter listing with a small max_keys and proves no key or common prefix is duplicated or missed.
answer_hinglish:
Pagination with delimiter tricky hai kyunki ek page contents (keys) aur common_prefixes (folders) dono count karta hai, aur ek "folder" ke andar hazaron keys ho sakti hain jinhe skip karna hai. `list_objects` folder milne pe `after = cp + "\U0010ffff"` set karta hai taaki next query us folder ki saari keys ke aage se shuru ho, aur truncate hone pe `next_start_after` return karta hai. Bug ka classic form: ek prefix do pages pe repeat ho jaye, ya page boundary pe ek key chhoot jaye.

Test strategy: ground truth ek single `max_keys=1000` call se lo, phir `max_keys=2` se loop chalao jab tak `is_truncated` false na ho, har page ke contents aur prefixes collect karo, aur assert karo (1) concatenation ground truth ke barabar hai, (2) koi duplicate nahi, (3) loop bounded hai (infinite loop guard).

Keys aisi chuno jo edge cases maaren: folder pehli position pe, folder page boundary pe, ek folder ke andar subfolder, aur `%`/`_` wali key (LIKE escaping). Observation (O8): ordering DB collation pe depend karti hai; test ground truth se compare karta hai isliye collation-independent hai.
why_needed: Listing pagination bugs silent hote hain -- client ko kuch keys kabhi dikhti hi nahi; property-style test unhe pakadta hai.
real_world_analogy: Kitaab ke index ko 2-2 entries karke padhna aur check karna ki poore index se koi entry chhooti ya dohrai to nahi.
how_it_works: Har page: `GET /buckets/b/objects?delimiter=/&max_keys=2&start_after=<prev next_start_after>`. Result keys + prefixes ko list mein append. Loop guard: max 50 iterations.
in_this_project: `objstore/services/objects.py::list_objects` aur route `objstore/api/routes.py::list_objects` (`max_keys` 1..1000). Existing `test_listing_prefix_delimiter_pagination` sirf bina delimiter ke 2 pages check karta hai -- yeh test delimiter + many pages cover karta hai.
code_example:
# solution: tests/test_objects.py (new test)
async def test_delimiter_pagination_no_dupes_no_gaps(db, tmp_path):
    async with server(tmp_path) as (app, cl, anon):
        a = cl["alice"]
        await bucket(a)
        keys = ["a/1", "a/2", "b.txt", "c/x/1", "c/y", "d.txt", "e/1", "f_%.txt", "g.txt"]
        for k in keys:
            await a.put("photos", k, b"x")
        url = "/buckets/photos/objects"
        full = (await a.request("GET", url, params={"delimiter": "/"})).json()
        truth = [c["key"] for c in full["contents"]] + full["common_prefixes"]

        seen, start = [], ""
        for _ in range(50):
            p = {"delimiter": "/", "max_keys": "2"}
            if start:
                p["start_after"] = start
            page = (await a.request("GET", url, params=p)).json()
            seen += [c["key"] for c in page["contents"]] + page["common_prefixes"]
            if not page["is_truncated"]:
                break
            start = page["next_start_after"]
        else:
            raise AssertionError("pagination did not terminate")
        assert len(seen) == len(set(seen)), seen
        assert sorted(seen) == sorted(truth)
        assert set(full["common_prefixes"]) == {"a/", "c/", "e/"}

Real DB required

Termination guard na rakhna
Prefixes ko count mein na ginna

question: The 7-day presign limit used to be checked only when the URL was created. How is it enforced at verification time now, and how is it tested?
answer_hinglish:
Review finding O1 (fixed): `/presign` route `expires_in > cfg.max_presign_seconds` pe 422 deta hai, lekin `auth._presigned` sirf `int(expires) < time.time()` check karta tha. Presigning ek pure client-side HMAC operation hai -- `signing.presign()` ko koi bhi jiske paas secret hai call kar sakta hai, server ke `/presign` endpoint ke bina. Toh ek SDK ya leaked secret wala attacker 10 saal valid URL bana sakta hai, aur woh URL key revoke hone tak chalega. Policy jo sirf ek optional endpoint pe enforce ho, woh policy nahi hai.

Shipped fix: verification pe `exp > time.time() + max_age + 60` (60s skew margin) -> 401 'presigned URL expiry exceeds the maximum'. Regression test `test_presigned_url_with_excessive_expiry_is_rejected_at_use`. Max value ka source settings hai; `_presigned` ke paas `request` hai, toh `request.app.state.settings.max_presign_seconds` padh sakte hain -- signature badalne ki zaroorat nahi. Real AWS bhi yahi karta hai: `X-Amz-Expires` max 604800 seconds verify time pe reject hota hai.

Ek aur subtle baat: URL mein issue time nahi hai, sirf absolute expiry hai. Isliye hum "lifetime" nahi, "remaining lifetime" check kar sakte hain -- jo kaafi hai, kyunki 7 din se aage ki expiry wala URL abhi turant reject ho jayega.
why_needed: Security limits server pe har request ke time enforce hone chahiye, kisi ek convenience endpoint pe nahi.
real_world_analogy: Visitor pass ki validity security guard gate pe check karta hai, sirf reception pe nahi -- warna koi khud pass chhaap le.

question: Write a test proving that concurrent PUTs into a bucket with a quota can never push stored bytes over the quota.
answer_hinglish:
Quota check classic check-then-act race hai: do concurrent PUTs dono `SELECT sum(size)` padhte hain = 600, dono sochte hain 300 aur add ho sakta hai (900 <= 1000), dono insert karte hain -> 1200. Project yeh `SELECT 1 FROM buckets WHERE name = :b FOR UPDATE` se rokta hai -- quota wale bucket ke saare writers commit pe serialize hote hain, aur check + insert same transaction mein lock ke andar hain. Lock sirf `quota_bytes is not None` hone pe liya jata hai (bucket-lock bottleneck fix, TESTING.md: 53 -> 72 PUT/s).

Test: quota 1000 bytes, 10 alag keys pe 300-300 bytes ke 10 PUTs `asyncio.gather` se ek saath. Sahi behaviour: exactly 3 succeed (900), baaki 7 ko 403 QuotaExceeded. Assert: 200 count == 3, DB mein `sum(size) <= 1000`, stats ka `stored_bytes == 900`, aur disk pe sirf 3 blobs (rejected uploads ke blobs `except BaseException` branch delete karti hai).

Agar koi future refactor lock hata de, toh yeh test (ASGI in-process, real Postgres, concurrency) usually fail karega -- race tests probabilistic hote hain, lekin 10 parallel writers ke saath window kaafi badi hai. Review mein yahi gap multipart ke liye mila tha (O2: `upload_part` lock nahi leta tha) -- fix ke baad `test_multipart_parts_respect_quota_and_completion_check_is_real` parts ke liye bhi quota assert karta hai.
why_needed: Quota bypass = billing/abuse problem; concurrency bugs sirf concurrent tests se pakde jaate hain.
real_world_analogy: Cinema mein last 3 seats: do counters ek saath 'available' dekh ke ticket bech dein toh overbooking; ek central lock wala counter hi sahi hai.
how_it_works: put_object: stream blob -> txn: key advisory lock -> bucket FOR UPDATE (quota only) -> `_check_quota` sums objects + parts -> commit_version -> commit releases lock. Next writer lock milne pe naya sum dekhta hai.
in_this_project: `objstore/services/objects.py::put_object` aur `_check_quota`; existing `test_quota_counts_all_versions` sequential hai, aur `test_concurrent_writes_to_same_key` concurrency hai lekin bina quota. Yeh test dono ko combine karta hai, `db` fixture se direct SQL assert ke saath.

# solution: tests/test_objects.py (new test)
async def test_concurrent_puts_never_exceed_quota(db, tmp_path):
    async with server(tmp_path) as (app, cl, anon):
        a = cl["alice"]
        await bucket(a)
        await a.request("PUT", "/buckets/photos/quota", json={"quota_bytes": 1000})
        rs = await asyncio.gather(*[a.put("photos", f"k{i}", b"z" * 300) for i in range(10)])
        codes = sorted(r.status_code for r in rs)
        assert codes == [200] * 3 + [403] * 7, codes
        assert all(r.json()["error"]["code"] == "QuotaExceeded" for r in rs if r.status_code == 403)
        from sqlalchemy import text
        async with db() as s:
            assert await s.scalar(text("SELECT coalesce(sum(size), 0) FROM objects WHERE bucket = 'photos'")) == 900
        files = [p for p in (tmp_path / "blobs").glob("*/*/*") if not p.name.startswith(".tmp-")]
        assert len(files) == 3      # rejected blobs were cleaned up
advantages: Proves the FOR UPDATE lock matters
Also proves cleanup of rejected blobs
disadvantages: Probabilistic: race window may not always open on very slow machines
Needs real DB, slower than unit tests
common_mistakes: Same key pe test karna (advisory lock already serialize karega, quota lock prove nahi hoga)
Sirf status codes check karna, DB sum nahi
Sequential `for` loop se 'concurrency' test

question: Walk me through the overall architecture of your object storage system.
answer_hinglish:
Paanch parts hain. (1) FastAPI API (`objstore/main.py`, `api/routes.py`) -- buckets, objects, multipart, presign, admin routes. Stateless hai: koi in-memory coordination nahi, sirf ek 60s secret cache. (2) Auth layer (`services/auth.py`, `services/signing.py`) -- har request pe authenticate (signed header, presigned URL, ya anonymous) aur authorize (owner, grants, public_read, admin). (3) Metadata in Postgres -- buckets, objects (har version ek row), multipart uploads/parts, grants, lifecycle rules, blob_deletions queue. Transactions, partial unique index aur advisory locks se correctness. (4) Bytes in a StorageAdapter -- local filesystem (temp + fsync + rename, sharded dirs) ya koi bhi S3-compatible store via boto3; blobs random keys pe, object key se kabhi derive nahi. (5) Maintenance worker (`worker.py`) -- har 300s lifecycle rules aur GC.

PUT ka flow: verify signature -> authorize write -> bytes ko naye random blob mein stream (MD5 + SHA-256 + size limit on the fly) -> digests verify -> chhota transaction: key advisory lock, quota ho toh bucket lock + check, versions flip, insert -> 200 ETag + version id. Overwritten blobs queue mein jaate hain, GC baad mein delete karta hai.

GET: latest (ya versionId) row -> delete marker? 404 -> If-None-Match match? 304 -> Range? 206 -> storage se stream.

Core idea: metadata ke liye database ki guarantees, bytes ke liye sasta blob store, aur dono ke beech crash-safe ordering.
why_needed: Interviewer pehle big picture dekhna chahta hai -- components, responsibilities, aur data flow.
real_world_analogy: Library: catalogue (Postgres) batata hai kaunsi kitaab kis shelf number pe hai; godown (blob store) mein bas numbered boxes hain; librarian (worker) raat ko purane boxes saaf karta hai.
how_it_works: Request -> bpcommon middleware (request id, metrics, logs) -> route -> authenticate/authorize -> services (objects/maintenance) -> Postgres + StorageAdapter. Worker same services ko direct call karta hai, API ke through nahi.
in_this_project: `ARCHITECTURE.md` mein mermaid diagrams (components, PUT ordering, GET with Range). `objstore/main.py::make_storage` backend choose karta hai (`OBJ_STORAGE_BACKEND=local|s3`), `create_app` lifespan mein engine (pool_size=10, max_overflow=20) aur adapter set karta hai. Docker compose: postgres, seaweedfs, migrate, api, worker.

Bytes API process se guzarte hain (CPU)
JSON API, S3 wire protocol nahi

question: Why a pluggable StorageAdapter protocol, and how did you prove the abstraction works against a real S3 API?
answer_hinglish:
`StorageAdapter` ek `typing.Protocol` hai jisme paanch async methods hain: `put(blob_key, HashingStream) -> BlobInfo`, `get(blob_key, start, end)` (async byte iterator, range support ke saath), `delete`, `exists`, `list_older_than(seconds)`. Services sirf yahi interface jaante hain; koi `isinstance` ya backend-specific branch nahi. Protocol structural typing hai -- `LocalAdapter` aur `S3Adapter` ko inherit karne ki zaroorat nahi, bas methods match hone chahiye.

Interface narrow kyun hai? Kyunki metadata (naam, versions, ACLs) Postgres mein hai -- blob layer ko sirf "opaque bytes under random key" chahiye. Isse koi bhi backend chal jata hai: filesystem, AWS S3, MinIO, SeaweedFS, Ceph. Hashing aur size limit `HashingStream` mein hai, adapter ke bahar -- toh integrity logic ek hi jagah hai.

Proof: abstraction tab tak sirf theory hai jab tak doosra real implementation pass na kare. `tests/test_s3_adapter.py` wahi API flow (PUT, GET, Range, multipart, delete, GC) real SeaweedFS S3 endpoint ke against chalata hai, aur ek 20MB streaming upload jahan boto3 8MB threshold ke upar apna managed multipart use karta hai -- `_QueueReader` bounded queue (max ~8 chunks) se constant memory. Endpoint na ho toh tests skip hote hain (`pytestmark skipif`).

Leaky parts honestly: `delete_any` (GC helper for `.tmp-*` files) protocol mein nahi hai par dono adapters mein hai; aur `ensure_bucket` sirf S3 ke liye `hasattr` se call hota hai.
why_needed: Backend lock-in avoid karna, local dev simple rakhna, aur production mein managed durable storage use karna.
real_world_analogy: Mobile charger ka USB-C port: phone ko farak nahi padta ki power wall socket se aa rahi hai ya power bank se, jab tak plug standard hai.
how_it_works: `put` stream consume karta hai (jo hashing karta hai), `stream.info()` return karta hai. `get` local pe seek + chunked read, S3 pe `Range` header ke saath `get_object`. GC `list_older_than` + `delete_any` use karta hai.
in_this_project: `objstore/storage/base.py::StorageAdapter` aur `HashingStream`; `storage/local.py::LocalAdapter`; `storage/s3.py::S3Adapter` + `_QueueReader`. Tests: `test_full_flow_on_s3_backend`, `test_large_streaming_upload_over_8mb_uses_s3_multipart`. TESTING.md benchmarks dono backends ke liye: 64MB PUT 153 MB/s local vs 45 MB/s S3 (SeaweedFS in Docker on Windows).

    async def put(self, blob_key: str, stream: HashingStream) -> BlobInfo: ...
    async def get(self, blob_key: str, start: int = 0, end: int | None = None) -> AsyncIterator[bytes]: ...
    async def delete(self, blob_key: str) -> None: ...
    async def exists(self, blob_key: str) -> bool: ...
    async def list_older_than(self, seconds: float) -> list[str]: ...

Proven against a real S3 implementation

delete_any/ensure_bucket protocol ke bahar
boto3 sync -> thread hops

Sirf mocks se abstraction 'prove' karna

question: Design an S3-like object storage service from scratch. What are the key components and decisions?
answer_hinglish:
Main isko teen planes mein baant ke design karta hoon, aur mere project ke decisions as reference.

1. Front/API plane: stateless HTTP servers, auth (HMAC signed requests, presigned URLs), rate limits. Horizontally scale. Mere project mein FastAPI + `authenticate/authorize`.

2. Metadata plane: bucket -> key -> versions, ACLs, multipart state, lifecycle. Requirements: strong consistency per key (read-after-write), ordered prefix listing, transactions for version flips. Chhote scale pe ek Postgres (mera choice: partial unique index for one-latest-per-key, advisory lock per key). Bade scale pe sharded metadata (bucket ya hash(bucket,key) se) -- jaise S3 ka internal index, ya FoundationDB/Spanner jaisa ordered transactional KV.

3. Data plane: bytes in immutable blobs under random ids, replication/erasure coding, scrubbing. Mera project yeh S3-compatible backend ko delegate karta hai.

Key decisions jo main highlight karta hoon: (a) bytes first, metadata second -- crash = orphan garbage, never dangling pointers; GC with grace period. (b) deletions async via queue. (c) end-to-end integrity: MD5/SHA-256 computed while streaming, Content-MD5 and signed payload checked. (d) multipart for big objects, ranges for resumable downloads. (e) versioning with delete markers. (f) lifecycle for cost.

Scale numbers (generic ballpark): metadata ops har request pe hote hain, bytes sirf data requests pe -- isliye metadata usually pehla bottleneck hai. Bytes ko API se bypass karne ke liye presigned URLs directly blob tier/CDN ko.
why_needed: Classic system design question; candidate ko metadata/data separation, consistency, durability aur scale reasoning dikhana hota hai.
real_world_analogy: Airport: check-in counter (API), central booking system (metadata), baggage handling (data plane) -- bags ka tag number random hai, naam se nahi.
how_it_works: PUT: API -> auth -> data plane write (placement, replicas) -> metadata commit (version flip) -> ack. GET: metadata lookup -> data plane read (ranged) -> stream. Background: GC, lifecycle, scrubbing, rebalancing.
in_this_project: Mere project mein data plane ke alawa sab real hai: `services/objects.py` (put/get/delete/list/multipart), `migrations/versions/0001_initial.py` (schema + `uq_objects_latest`), `services/maintenance.py` (lifecycle + GC), `storage/*` (adapters). `SYSTEM_DESIGN.md` scaling table: 10x more API processes + read replicas; 100x shard metadata, dedicated listing index, CDN, presign direct to blob store.

disadvantages: Metadata sharding hard (listing across shards)
Own data plane = big operational cost
Many moving parts

Metadata first likhna
Consistency requirement na batana

question: Why is the API stateless, and what exactly makes horizontal scaling safe?
answer_hinglish:
API process mein koi aisi state nahi jo correctness ke liye zaroori ho. Saari coordination Postgres mein hai: same-key writers `pg_advisory_xact_lock` pe serialize hote hain (yeh lock DB ka hai, process ka nahi, toh 2 instance hon ya 20 -- lock same hai); one-latest-per-key `uq_objects_latest` partial unique index enforce karta hai; quota ke liye bucket row `FOR UPDATE`. Bytes shared storage mein hain (S3 backend ya shared volume). Isliye load balancer kisi bhi request ko kisi bhi instance pe bhej sakta hai -- koi sticky session nahi.

Read-after-write consistency bhi isi se aati hai: PUT ka 200 metadata COMMIT ke baad jata hai, toh agla GET kisi bhi instance pe ho, woh primary se latest row padhega.

Ek hi per-instance state hai: `app.state.secret_cache` (`SecretCache`, 60s TTL). Yeh correctness nahi, sirf performance hai -- cost: revoke kiya hua key har instance pe 60s tak chal sakta hai (TRADEOFFS.md #10).

Caveats: local adapter ke saath horizontal scaling ke liye blob root shared hona chahiye -- isliye compose S3 backend (SeaweedFS) use karta hai. Aur TESTING.md finding: ek Python process c=4 pe CPU-bound ho jata hai (76 PUT/s, CPU 122% of wall), toh throughput ka answer "zyada processes" hi hai -- jo statelessness ki wajah se possible hai.
why_needed: Throughput badhane ka sabse sasta tareeka replicas hain; woh tabhi safe hai jab instances ke beech koi hidden shared state na ho.
real_world_analogy: Bank ke kai cashier counters: sab ek hi central ledger mein entry karte hain, toh customer kisi bhi counter pe jaa sakta hai.
how_it_works: Instance A aur B dono same key pe PUT: dono apna blob likhte hain (parallel), phir commit pe DB advisory lock pe line lagate hain, ek ke baad ek version flip. Unique index last line of defence.
in_this_project: `objstore/services/objects.py::key_lock_sql` (`pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended(:b || '/' || :k, 0))`), `objstore/services/auth.py::_secret` (cache), `DEPLOYMENT.md`: "The API is stateless: run as many replicas as needed behind a load balancer." `docker-compose.yml` default backend `s3`.

    return "SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended(:b || '/' || :k, 0))"

question: Why do lifecycle and garbage collection run in a separate worker instead of inside API requests?
answer_hinglish:
Teen reasons. (1) Latency aur reliability: request path ko blob delete ya bulk lifecycle SQL ka wait nahi karna chahiye. DELETE request sirf metadata change + `blob_deletions` queue insert karta hai, aur turant return; blob store slow ya down ho toh bhi user ka delete succeed hota hai. (2) Time-based kaam: lifecycle "30 din purane logs expire karo" kisi request se trigger nahi hota -- kisi ko periodically check karna hai. (3) Isolation: GC ka orphan scan poora blob store list karta hai -- heavy work API ke event loop pe nahi hona chahiye.

`objstore/worker.py` ek simple loop hai: har 300 seconds `run_lifecycle` phir `run_gc`; exception pe `maintenance_failed` log karke agle cycle pe retry. Same container image, alag command (`python -m objstore.worker`).

Multiple workers safe hain (worker docstring): lifecycle idempotent hai (doosri baar kuch extra nahi karta -- `test_lifecycle_expiration_noncurrent_and_markers` third run pe saare counters 0 assert karta hai), aur GC delete se pehle reference re-check karta hai. Lekin duplicate work hota hai -- production mein ek leader (advisory lock) ya sharding behtar.

Admins ke liye `POST /admin/lifecycle/run` aur `/admin/gc/run` bhi hain -- tests aur manual ops ke liye, same functions call karte hain.
why_needed: Background maintenance ko user-facing path se alag rakhna latency, failure isolation aur time-based scheduling deta hai.
real_world_analogy: Restaurant ke waiters customers serve karte hain; bartan dhone wala staff peeche alag kaam karta hai -- waiter har plate dhone nahi rukta.
how_it_works: Worker loop: lifecycle (per rule: expire current via delete_object, noncurrent via lag(), lone markers, abort old multipart) -> GC (queued deletions with re-check, orphan scan with grace) -> sleep 300.
in_this_project: `objstore/worker.py::main` (interval 300), `objstore/services/maintenance.py::run_lifecycle` aur `run_gc`, admin routes `lifecycle_run` / `gc_run` in `objstore/api/routes.py`. Compose mein `worker` service `command: ["python", "-m", "objstore.worker"]`. DEPLOYMENT.md: "alert if blob_deletions grows or GC fails".

disadvantages: Storage reclaimed late (eventual)

Multiple workers duplicate work

question: How would you take this to multiple regions with a CDN in front of public reads?
answer_hinglish:
Seedha: is project mein multi-region, cross-region replication aur CDN integration implement nahi hai; yeh single-region, single-Postgres design hai. SYSTEM_DESIGN.md 100x step mein "CDN in front of public reads" aur "presigned URLs pointing directly at the blob store" suggest karta hai. Production mein aise karte:

CDN (sabse pehla, sabse sasta win): public_read bucket objects immutable-per-version hain aur ETag strong hai, toh CDN cache kar sakta hai. Cache key mein versionId ho; latest-key URLs ke liye short TTL ya overwrite/delete pe purge. Private objects ke liye CDN signed URLs (presign jaisa) -- API sirf URL sign kare, bytes CDN/edge se. Range requests (206) CDN support karte hain.

Multi-region: do models. (a) Home region per bucket: metadata aur writes ek region mein (strong consistency wahin), aur async cross-region replication (CRR) se doosre region mein read copies -- doosre region ke reads eventually consistent. Replication ek queue se: commit ke saath outbox row likho, replicator bytes copy kare, phir remote metadata likhe -- yahan bhi bytes first, metadata second rule chalega. (b) Active-active: conflicting writes same key pe -- last-writer-wins by timestamp/version, jo complex aur lossy hai; zyada tar systems (S3 bhi) per-bucket home region rakhte hain.

Failover: home region down toh replica promote, lekin replication lag ka data RPO ke roop mein jaa sakta hai -- yeh honestly batana zaroori hai.
why_needed: Global users ke liye latency, aur region outage se survive karne ke liye disaster recovery.
real_world_analogy: Head office (home region) mein master register, branch offices mein photocopy jo har ghante update hoti hai; dukaan ke bahar vending machine (CDN) popular cheezein turant deti hai.
how_it_works: Write: home region API -> blob -> metadata commit + replication outbox row (same txn). Replicator: read outbox -> copy blob to remote -> remote metadata upsert (idempotent by version_id) -> mark done. Reads: nearest region; strong reads home region se.
in_this_project: Hooks jo already hain: `objects.version_id` (replication idempotency key), `sha256` (remote copy verify), `blob_deletions` jaisa queue pattern outbox ke liye, aur `/presign` (`objstore/api/routes.py::presign`) jo `public_base_url` embed karta hai -- CDN domain set karna wahin se. `objstore/api/routes.py::get_object` `ETag`, `Last-Modified`, `Accept-Ranges` headers already deta hai jo CDN caching ke liye zaroori hain.
advantages: CDN offloads public read bytes completely
Home-region model keeps strong consistency per bucket
Existing version ids make replication idempotent
disadvantages: Cross-region replicas eventually consistent
Failover can lose recent writes (RPO)
Purge/invalidations for latest-key URLs
common_mistakes: Active-active ko 'free consistency' samajhna
Mutable latest-key URLs ko long TTL pe cache karna
Replication mein metadata pehle copy karna (remote dangling pointer)
follow_up_questions: How would you invalidate CDN caches on overwrite?
What is the RPO/RTO of async cross-region replication?
How would you replicate delete markers and permanent version deletes?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Home-region: simple + strong per bucket, lekin far users ke writes slow. Active-active: low latency writes, conflicts aur complexity.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Region outage during replication lag -> recent objects missing in replica; replicator bug -> silent divergence (sha256 compare se detect).
advanced.alternatives: Backend-level replication (S3 CRR / MinIO site replication) for bytes + Postgres logical replication for metadata; global DB (Spanner/CockroachDB) for metadata.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 100x reads: CDN hit ratio sabse bada lever; 100x writes: metadata sharding pehle, regions baad mein.
advanced.production_improvements: Replication lag metrics + alerts, periodic cross-region checksum audits, documented RPO/RTO, CDN cache keys with versionId.
